articles.title: Meet the tiny wild cat that’s new to science
articles.summary: A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
articles.body: A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century. The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger cats found across much ​of South America. It was found in Bolivia’s lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18 inches (46 cm) long and weighs around 3 pounds (1.4 kg), making it smaller than the average domestic cat. Researchers used genetic data to confirm that ⁠the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name. “Its fur is light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic Explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology. Little is yet known about ⁠the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. Tiger cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium. Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence ‌of multiple species. Referring to the new species, Lescroart said, “Our information at ⁠this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.” One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home. ‘A different animal’ Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?” The team analyzed DNA from 38 cats ​sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species. “We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat ​to be a ‌separate species, and no one had ever ​proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said. Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago. “The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap ⁠is generally considered a species-level divide in cats. The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s ​Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region ofthe old Inca Empire that included the area it inhabits. The International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, Red List tracking the status ​of species currently treats tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species ⁠with declining populations. The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could potentially be considered endangered when assessed on their own. The need for a ⁠clearer assessment ‌is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the region’s most threatened ecosystems. The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent ‌priorities, Nogales-Ascarrunz ‌added. “Showing the general public ​that even ​in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

articles.title: Lost Bowie tracks from 1960s released for first time
articles.summary: Previously unheard material from the start of the artist's career has been released for the first time.
articles.body:
Ten years ago Alec Palao was casually flicking through a collection of old records when he noticed some faint pencil markings that were enough to draw a gasp. "Davie Jones," it read.

What he had found was musical gold: five unreleased songs by a young David Bowie, filed away under his birth name.

From Friday, those tracks, plus another five unreleased songs that came Palao's way after the initial discovery, will be available to buy and stream.

"They are probably the most visceral, raw you'll ever hear the man," said Palao, a music historian and archivist.

For the music industry, David Bowie is big business. He entered the mainstream with his 1969 single, Space Oddity, and went on to achieve 11 number one albums.

He died in 2016, but remains one of Britain's most recognisable cultural icons.

Six of the previously unreleased tracks from the new collection will be available on vinyl, tapping into Bowie's popularity in that format specifically. In 2022, Bowie was named the best-selling vinyl artist of the 21st century by Music Week, ahead of The Beatles.

"It's just a fascinating window into London in 1965 and its possibilities," said Palao.

In the early sixties, Bowie was a teenager, performing as Davie Jones at London clubs and dreaming of stardom. Many of the tracks he recorded in that period are either little known or lost to time.

But his first professional producer, Shel Talmy, had kept a recording from 1965 among his collection of material by other artists he had worked with: The Kinks; The Who; Manfred Mann; The Easybeats.

It was within Talmy's collection that Palao came across the valuable 12-inch acetate.

That material and the five other previously unheard tunes, as well as demos and remastered songs, form part of a new, posthumous album called The Shel Talmy Recordings.

A limited edition vinyl will be sold at Record Store Day and HMV outlets.

In 2022, David Bowie's estate sold the publishing rights to decades of the singer's work to Warner Music Group. For this new material, Palao, along with Talmy Enterprises Incorporated, licensed the album to Warner, and it will be released by the company's subsidiary, Parlophone. Royalties will be paid to Bowie's estate by Warner.

"I think it's wonderful that people can get to hear the early Davie Jones music," said Dana Gillespie, an early collaborator of Bowie's.

She met him after a performance at the Marquee Club in London when Bowie was 17.

"They're songs that don't really sound like David but it's him trying to find his voice. He was experimenting."

Gillespie became close friends with Bowie, eventually working with him on his "Ziggy Stardust" album. Talmy worked with both artists and Bowie's song "Andy Warhol", on his fourth studio album, was originally written for Gillespie.

"He was very driven," remembered Gillespie, who is still touring and making music at the age of 77.

"Some time in the sixties, he asked me to come and visit his parents. We were in his little house in Bromley, and when his parents left the room he turned to me and said: 'Whatever it takes, I want to get out of here.' And he did," she said.

It is a decade since Palao found the recordings. Since then, it has been a long process to bring them to market. The result is an album that he says is "absolutely pure rock 'n' roll".

"If you're looking for clues as to what he was to become, there's maybe less of that," said Palao, "but objectively speaking, I feel it's important stuff."

Gillespie is excited by one song in particular.

"There was a famous café called the Gioconda in Denmark Street where I often used to go with David," she said, recalling the centre of musical life in London in the 1960s.

"One day when I was sitting there, David rushed in and took me by the hand. He said: 'You have to hear this'.

"He ran with me around the corner and squeezed us into a small listening booth. I had one speaker and he had the other, and he played me 'I Pity The Fool'."

A remastered version of the song can be heard in the new album.

For music historians, fans of Bowie, and those who were there, the new album is another chance to reconnect with an enduring cultural icon.

"David always wanted to be a big star," said Gillespie. "I'm so happy that his early stuff hasn't been forgotten."

articles.title: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
articles.summary: The military and government say the risk of conflict is growing, but we may not be mentally ready for it
articles.body:
If the UK suddenly found itself at war, would you know what to do? Do you know what would be expected of you?

The Government wants us all to start preparing for severe disruption to our lives. It wants us to stockpile canned food and drinking water, strengthen our civic resilience, and plan for the possibility of war.

Work has begun on the government's so-called "war book", which hasn't been updated in decades.

The UK's most senior soldier has sounded the alarm. The Chief of the Defence Staff Sir Richard Knighton this week said the threat from Russia meant Britain was living through the "most dangerous" period of his 35-year career in the armed forces.

But what is the threat? In 1940 the danger of a German invasion of the UK was very real. But the chances of Russian tanks rolling up Whitehall are surely negligible.

"It's not the tanks you need to worry about," says historian Margaret MacMillan, author of War: How Conflict Shaped Us.

"It's the cutting of cables on the ocean floor. It's the hacking into systems on which so many things depend. The possibility for asymmetric war, for cyber war, is growing by leaps and bounds."

But are we ready? After 80 years without war on our own soil, are we, as a society, psychologically prepared for it? Are we ready to approve large increases in defence spending, and for the sacrifices that that might entail in other areas of our national life? Or does the threat seem too far-fetched to be real?

"I think we have become used to the idea that peace is the normal state of affairs, that it's going to last," says McMillan.

"So no, I don't think we are psychologically prepared… but I do think that we are beginning to recognise that war is something that is closer to us than we'd like to think".

Archive film footage showing Britons in 1913 enjoying days at the races or watching the cricket contrasts sharply with what followed during the horrors of World War One.

"In a sense it's now a bit like those Edwardian summers before 1914, when there was a lot of talk of war but the notion of actually going to war seemed so far-fetched as to be beyond belief and I think that's where we are at the moment," says retired British General Sir Richard Shirreff, a former Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe.

Europe has not always been so war-averse. In 1914, recruitment stations were flooded with volunteers eager to serve their country. In Britain, that generation was raised on heroic tales of empire-building, in which war was one glorious cavalry charge, leading to swift victory and everyone home by Christmas.

But the experience of what came to be known as the Great War seared itself into the popular consciousness and survives in our collective imagination.

One in eight of the men who enlisted in the UK left their bones in the fields of Flanders and France, Mesopotamia and Gallipoli. The survivors carved their unspeakable grief into the landscape with the erection of thousands of war memorials. The pain of it touched every community in the land.

That conflict, says Margaret MacMillan, changed fundamentally the way Europe thought about war.

"The experience of the First World War showed just how dreadful modern war is… And the idea that war could be glamorous never really came back after that."

Europeans, and especially Western Europe's leadership elites, have succumbed to a decades-long "crisis of disbelief", argues Andrew Michta, a Polish-born American academic who is professor of strategic studies at the Hamilton School, University of Florida.

He argues that the UK, in common with many European nations, has very low levels of psychological preparedness, and that authorities are not being candid about the looming threats.

"The Germans have totally disarmed during the last 30 years. The UK is also largely disarmed and, most importantly, mentally. There is no readiness for what's happening because the policy elites are not addressing their publics in a way that would honestly state the gravity of the situation," Michta says.

When the Soviet Union collapsed in the early 1990s, many European countries began a decades-long winding down of military preparedness, dramatically cutting defence spending, in the belief that the threat from Russia had disappeared.

Michta singles out Germany's heavy reliance on Russian energy via the Nord Stream gas pipelines - which transported huge quantities of gas from Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea - in what he sees as the mistaken belief that Berlin could manage its relationship with Moscow via political and economic means.

"So you've lived through 20 years of appeasement in Europe driven by the elites' lack of willingness or courage… to articulate how the situation was changing and how rapidly."

General Sir Richard Shirreff argues that Russia's initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014 was the real turning point, the moment Russia revealed itself as a tenacious threat to western security.

"The reality is that Russia believes it's been at war with Nato since 2014. Not a conventional war, but a war designed to undermine the integrity of target states or alliances.

"I would never take the Russians for granted. It would not be beyond the realms of possibility for them to try to unhinge Nato by, for example, attempting to take over Spitsbergen [in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard] or something else indirect.

"So that's what we need to be prepared for".

Mounting calls for increases in defence spending are rooted in a belief that the best way to prevent a war is to be ready - psychologically and militarily - to fight one. Not everyone agrees.

The belief that we are under threat is key, says psychologist Jim Orford, professor emeritus of clinical and community psychology at the University of Birmingham. "It is what I call simplistic thinking. In order to contemplate the possibility of going to war we've got to think in simplistic terms. In terms of enemies and heroes. We've got to think of Russia as an enemy. The narratives are all simplified.

"Being [psychologically] prepared for war is the first stage. Contemplating war is the second phase and then actually engaging in war is the third. I think we're well into the 'contemplating war' phase."

This "crisis of disbelief", as Michta put it, is not evenly spread. The further east you go, the closer you get to the Russian border, the more alert a nation's people are to the threat, and the more psychologically prepared.

Sweden hasn't had a war in 200 years. It has pursued a policy of neutrality for centuries. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it abandoned that and has made itself, in a very short space of time, one of the most psychologically prepared countries in Europe.

"Russia is self-evidently dangerous", Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Christersson told The Economist magazine last month.

"We don't know when it [the war in Ukraine] ends, but how it ends will define the security situation in our part of the world for at least a generation"

Sweden has a system of partial conscription, in which all school leavers must register for military service. The armed forces pick - and conscript - the best candidates. The conscripts then do up to 15 months compulsory training before going back into civilian life, in employment or higher education. At the same time, they become part of their country's large reserve force.

"There's a lot of citizen engagement," says Minna Alander, an analyst at the Stockholm Centre for Eastern European Studies think tank. "It was almost an internet joke in 2022 and 2023 that everybody wished for a call up. Sometimes people get frustrated if they haven't been called up for a long time. It's an expectation for sure.

"Sweden has, for example, been identifying civil engineers with some relevant skills in, say, electricity supply who could be exercised in case of disruption. So Sweden can access this pool of civil engineers [who know] what they could do and how they could be activated."

When Christersson was asked whether Russia should be seen as a potential aggressor even after the war in Ukraine is over he said, "Yes. We have a few hundred years experience of this… We know Russia pretty well."

The three Baltic Republics - Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia - also know Russia pretty well. They only regained their independence from Moscow in the 1990s. German troops invaded Lithuania in the 1940s and are now back on Lithuanian soil, this time by invitation, to bolster that country's defences against the threat from the east. A thousand British troops lead a multi-national force in Estonia for the same reason.

But it is to the Finns that much of Europe now looks for lessons in mass psychological preparedness and civic resilience.

Finland's approach to defence and security is also rooted in historical experience. Of the 100,000 Nordic citizens who died in the World War Two, 90% were from Finland. They died in the so-called Winter War of 1939-40 against the Soviet Union. This tiny country repelled an attack by its giant neighbour and retained its independence.

Finland today shares an 800-mile (1,287km) border with Russia. After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Finland also quickly abandoned its historic neutrality and joined Nato along with its neighbour Sweden.

Finland has universal male conscription, and some women also volunteer to serve. When their service is complete they then become part of Finland's reserve force. This has the effect of closing the gap between the professional military and the civilian population.

"If conscription is done well, it ties every single family into national security thinking. Your grandfather, your great-grandfather and your sons, they all go to the same military service," says the retired three-star General Arto Raty, a former permanent secretary of Finland's Ministry of Defence.

"We bind the whole of society into supporting the military. Every single hospital has its crisis tasking. Every water supply agency. And interestingly, the most publicly trusted organisations in Finland today are the military, the defence forces and the police. That is not the case in most countries."

The Finnish military also runs a series of courses annually for leaders of society - MPs, government ministers, the CEOs of private enterprises and public utilities, the health service, even NGOs and the churches.

"We train them in crisis management, so that they understand how society will work in a crisis. We've been doing it every year since 1960."

Finland, with a population of 5.5 million, has a professional defence force of 23,000. That compares to Britain's 70,000 from a population of 66 million. But it also has a trained reserve force of close to 1 million and can mobilise a reserve army of 280,000 at short notice.

In 2025, Finland spent 2.5% of its GDP on defence, comparable to the 2.3% spent by the UK the same year.

Should the rest of Europe go to the expense of following Finland's lead when the prospects of a conventional war with Russia seem vanishingly remote?

"An army of 70,000 is simply not going to cut the mustard in the sort of war we are going to have to face," says Gen Sir Richard Shirreff. "So I don't see how we could generate the military capability needed without some form of call-up."

He says the Norwegian model might be one that helps change the British mindset around war.

"There, every school leaver is registered for conscription… and they go and do a year's training after which they go on to university and when, later, they are competing for jobs, if they've got national service on their CV, they're seen as the best candidates… That's the sort of thing we should look at."

He adds: "The case has to be made honestly by political leaders who must really look the population in the eye and say 'this has got to be done for us to be secure'."

articles.title: Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger quietly rolls back Youngkin's plans to protect girls' sports
articles.summary: Abigail Spanberger's administration quietly withdrew proposed protections for girls' sports and female spaces like locker rooms and bathrooms in Virginia.
articles.body: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's administration quietly rolled back proposed protections for girls' sports in the state, without announcing it to the public. Spanberger’s administration withdrew a proposed regulation that would have prevented biological males from competing on female-only athletic teams and entering certain female-designated spaces, including locker rooms and bathrooms. The withdrawal occurred July 30, 2026, but received little public attention until September. The administration did not issue a news release or publicly announce the decision. THE STATES THAT STILL ALLOW TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS FACE QUESTIONS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING The change appeared instead on the Virginia Regulatory Town Hall website, which lists the proposed regulations as having been "withdrawn on 07/30/2026 after the comment period had ended." OutKick has reached out to Spanberger's office for an explanation, but has not received a response. The proposal had not yet become a finalized regulation. Its withdrawal ended the rulemaking process initiated under former Republican Gov. Glenn Youngkin. The effort began with a petition filed in April 2025 by female athletes Réka György, Lily Mullens and Carter Satterfield. The petition asked the Virginia State Board of Health to adopt regulations barring biological males from female-only athletic teams and competitions, as well as female spaces in which women and girls could be undressed. The Virginia High School League changed its eligibility policy in February 2025 to restrict participation in girls’ sports to students whose biological sex is female. The organization oversees most public high school athletic competitions in Virginia. Virginia’s Department of Education also issued model policies under Youngkin in 2023 directing public schools to generally separate athletic teams and intimate facilities on the basis of biological sex. Those policies state that school divisions should provide reasonable accommodations to students while preserving the availability of sex-separated bathrooms, locker rooms and other facilities. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Implementation of the state’s model policies has varied among local school divisions, contributing to a prolonged dispute over transgender policies in Virginia schools. The issue has been especially contentious in Northern Virginia, where disagreements over bathrooms, locker rooms, pronouns and parental notification have prompted clashes between state officials and local school boards. The withdrawn Board of Health action would have established a separate regulatory framework reaching organized female sports and sex-separated spaces across Virginia. With the July 30 withdrawal, there are no remaining actions listed under the proposed regulatory chapter. The athletes argued that the participation of biological males in women’s sports and their access to female-designated facilities created physical and psychological harms for women and girls. In August 2025, the Board of Health unanimously approved the petition by a 14-0 vote and authorized the state to begin developing the regulations. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP According to the state’s regulatory website, the proposed rules were intended to "prevent biological males from participating in organized female-only athletic teams and competitions in Virginia" and from entering designated female spaces where women and girls were likely to be in a state of undress.

articles.title: Badenoch brings in lawyers after 94% Wandsworth Council tax hike
articles.summary: A row is growing over Wandsworth Council's rise, which the local authority is blaming on government funding cuts.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record council tax rise in one of her party's flagship local authorities.

She told BBC Newsnight the proposed 94% hike in Wandsworth, a south-west London borough run by the Tories, was "outrageous".

Badenoch said the Conservative Party had "instructed lawyers" to explore if an £84m-a-year government funding cut, which Wandsworth Council has blamed for the increase, can be blocked.

The government has insisted it needs to reform the "outdated" council funding system to move money to where it is most needed.

Wandsworth has long had one of the lowest council tax rates in the country, with an average Band D property currently paying just over £1,000, compared to above £2,000 in an increasing number of London boroughs.

But this would nearly double with the planned £958 rise - half of which is set by the council and the other half the mayor of London.

There has been heavy criticism since the move was announced in a council meeting on Tuesday. A final decision is to be made early next year.

Commenting for the first time on the row, Badenoch accused ministers of seemingly "taking money from areas that don't vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour".

"I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth Council is having to put up council tax.

"But they're not doing it because they want to. It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding.

"So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative Party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision."

Pressed by presenter Matt Chorley on how the rise will still mean Wandsworth's council tax is lower than many councils across the country, Badenoch said it would still worry some families.

"I think if you suddenly have a nearly 100% increase in your council tax, you would be extremely worried. Families have budgets," she said.

"Just because on average it's lower than somewhere else doesn't mean that people are going to be able to afford it."

She refused to say what alternative rate of increase she would propose, but questioned why a 40% cut was being imposed on the council when "Andy Burnham has not found 40% of anything to cut" himself.

She also defended her record as local government minister when the Tories were in Downing Street, despite Conservative governments having slashed some council grants.

Changes to the funding formula for councils under the Fair Funding Review 2.0, will see money redistributed from some council areas to others.

After deciding to reduce their share of central government funding, the government gave five London boroughs - Kensington & Chelsea, Westminster, Wandsworth, Hammersmith & Fulham and the City of London - and Windsor and Maidenhead Council in Berkshire the power to raise council tax above the usual 5% cap for two years.

The London councils Kensington & Chelsea, Westminster and Hammersmith & Fulham are considering joining Wandsworth in using the Sustainable Communities Act to challenge the cuts.

Wandsworth Council's Tory deputy leader said on Tuesday: "Higher council tax will not be easy or welcome. We do not regard it as fair and will continue to challenge the government by every possible means."

Leader of the opposition, Labour councillor Simon Hogg, said: "It's outrageous, it is stunning. People who don't know how to run the council panicking and making you pay the price.

"This increase is unfair, it's unnecessary and we oppose it."

However, the PoliticsHome website reported that three Labour MPs in Wandsworth - Rosena Allin-Khan, Fleur Anderson and Marsha de Cordova - have refused to back the council's appeal to the government to stop the funding cuts.

The three Labour MPs claimed the council "was in a strong financial position" before the Tories took over at the May elections earlier this year.

In a statement when the council tax rise was announced, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "Local authorities decide the level of council tax they wish to set, but we are clear that in doing so they should put taxpayers first.

"We're fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest, while protecting councils through the transition and ensuring no area faces a cliff edge."

articles.title: What happened to Evelyn Lima Dantas? Brazilian TikToker shot and killed at 21
articles.summary: US Streamers News: A young Brazilian TikToker’s life came to a sudden and violent end after she was reportedly shot outside a home in northern Brazil. Evelyn Lima Dantas.
articles.body: A young Brazilian TikToker’s life came to a sudden and violent end after she was reportedly shot outside a home in northern Brazil. Evelyn Lima Dantas, 21, was found dead on Sept. 16 after police responded to reports of gunfire in Mãe do Rio. Her death has raised questions about a possible link to a criminal investigation that had already brought her into police custody earlier this year.TikToker Evelyn Lima Dantas was reportedly dragged from home before shootingAuthorities in Mãe do Rio were called early Wednesday after residents heard several gunshots. According to a police report obtained by Brazilian outlet g1, officers arrived at a residential area and found Dantas dead outside a home.Details from her family, as reported to Military Police, paint a disturbing picture of the final moments. Two men allegedly entered the house, took Dantas outside and shot her several times. They then reportedly left the scene in a car.Police also found the letters “TCP” spray-painted at the location. Authorities believe the initials may refer to Terceiro Comando Puro, a criminal faction in Brazil. However, that connection remains part of the investigation and has not been established as a confirmed motive for Dantas’ killing.The case has drawn attention in part because of Dantas’ online presence. She had built a combined audience of more than 150,000 followers on TikTok and her now-deactivated Instagram account. Her posts focused largely on lifestyle, beauty and fitness, giving followers a glimpse into her life away from the criminal investigation surrounding her death.Her TikTok account appeared to have been inactive since January 2025, when she shared a lip-sync video with another creator.Evelyn Lima Dantas’ arrest adds another layer to the investigationDantas’ recent history with authorities is now another key part of the case. According to the police report cited by g1, she was arrested in July while authorities were investigating the killing of a local police sergeant.She remained in police custody until Sept. 9, when she was released provisionally. Just one week later, she was killed.A Military Police commander said investigators are examining whether her death could have been connected to the earlier case. The official described a possible motive involving retaliation or an attempt to destroy evidence, while stressing that it is one of several investigative possibilities.“We are strongly working with the hypothesis of retaliation or destruction of evidence by some criminal faction,” a Military Police commander told reporters in Spanish of a possible connection between Dantas’s killing and her previous arrest, per g1. “This is one of the main priority lines of investigation and information that we have.”That theory has not been proven, and authorities have yet to publicly establish who was responsible for the killing or why Dantas was targeted.PEOPLE reported that it had contacted the Military Police for comment.As investigators work to piece together what happened, Dantas’ death remains under investigation. The circumstances surrounding her arrest, her release and the shooting are expected to be examined as authorities determine whether the events were connected or whether another motive was involved.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Latvia bars NHL’s Ovechkin, Trump Jr. wedding benefactor from entering country
articles.summary: Latvia has barred Washington Capitals star Alex Ovechkin from entering the country days after the he appeared in a political ad for a party backed by Russian President Vladimir Putin. “The Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, has decided to include Alexander Ovechkin and [International Boxing Association President] Umar Kremlev on the list of personae…
articles.body:
Latvia has barred Washington Capitals star Alex Ovechkin from entering the country days after the he appeared in a political ad for a party backed by Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“The Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, has decided to include Alexander Ovechkin and [International Boxing Association President] Umar Kremlev on the list of personae non gratae and to prohibit their entry into Latvia for an indefinite period,” the ministry said in a statement .

The ministry said Thursday the decision was made in accordance with Latvia’s immigration law but did not give a specific reason for barring the two Russian natives.

The two were placed on the Latvian persona non gratae list, which prohibits them from entering the country — a NATO member that borders Russia.

The announcement came the same day Ovechkin addressed his controversial appearance in an ad for United Russia, Putin’s ruling political party. The decision also closely followed reports that Kremlev helped finance wedding celebrations for President’s Trumps son, Donald Trump Jr., and his wife, Bettina.

The clip caused one House GOP member, Rep. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.), to ask NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman to investigate the Capital’s player for supporting the Russian president — who the lawmaker labeled a “criminal” partially due to his multi-year war in Ukraine.

When asked by reporters about the ad during the Capitals’ annual media day Thursday, Ovechkin responded, “I’m Russian, and I support my country.”

The NHL star added, “I’m for peace and love.”

When pressed on his decision to participate in the ad, Ovechkin, the NHL’s leading scorer, said he did not hesitate to do so. In the clip, the Capitals player stood behind Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in the ad and former Soviet hockey star Viacheslav Fetisov, among other prominent figures from the country.

“They asked me to do that. I say yes,” he said. “So it’s as simple as that.”

The 41-year-old has faced scrutiny over his relationship with Putin for years. In 2017, Ovechkin launched a movement called “Putin Team” in support of the Russian president.

Kremlev, the other sports figure added to Latvia’s banned list, has also been known to have close ties to Putin. His controversy-plagued International Boxing Association (IBA) is financed by Russia’s state-owned natural gas company, Gazprom.

Latvia, a European Union and NATO member, has barred numerous Russian nationals from entering the country since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. In 2025, Latvia ordered more than 800 Russian citizens to leave the country after failing to prove their Latvian language proficiency.

articles.title: Iran expels Swedish diplomat in retaliatory move
articles.summary: Tehran gives Swedish official 48 hours to leave as Iran says Stockholm is bowing down to outside pressure.
articles.body:
Iran has ordered a Swedish diplomat to leave the country one day after Sweden expelled an Iranian embassy official in Stockholm.

Sweden’s action was described by Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs as “unjustified” on Thursday.

“Without doubt, this action by the Swedish government is the result of the influence of the Zionist regime and an effort to disrupt the normal activities of the Islamic Republic of Iran’s Embassy in Stockholm,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement, Iran’s IRNA news agency reported.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry said its director general for Western Europe, Alireza Yousefi, summoned the Swedish ambassador in Tehran on Thursday. Yousefi protested Sweden’s policies, including its “⁠hosting of anti-Iranian terrorist elements and groups”.

The ministry said Iran would take necessary measures to safeguard its national rights and interests, including through reciprocal action.

IRNA reports that in response to Sweden’s actions, the ambassador was informed in the meeting that a Swedish diplomat in Tehran had been given 48 hours to leave Iran.

Sweden’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs announced on Wednesday that the Iranian official was asked to leave the country due to activity incompatible ‌with ⁠the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

The Vienna Convention defines ⁠the rules of ⁠diplomatic missions.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry also referenced Sweden’s obligations under international law, including the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, warning that disruption of the Iranian embassy’s duties would entail Sweden’s international responsibility, reported IRNA.

Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said the decision to expel the Iranian official was taken to protect Swedish citizens and interests.

Swedish Justice Minister Gunnar Strommer told state television that the decision involved Iran’s alleged activities against “Jewish and Israeli interests”.

“We know that Iran, over a long period of time, has conducted activities that threaten security in and against Sweden,” Strommer said, adding that Iran was “making use of criminal networks” to achieve its objectives.
